summary: Describes HOTP, an algorithm that turns a shared secret and a counter into one-time passwords using HMAC. It includes a security analysis and guidance on deploying it safely. It can be used in many places, from VPN logins to Wi-Fi sign-in and web transactions, and was written to encourage interoperable two-factor authentication.

plainLanguage.summary: HOTP lets a token and server calculate the same short code from a shared secret and a counter. The server must limit guesses and protect the secret, because the code is short and the counter can drift.

subtitle: How a shared secret and synchronized counter produce a short one-time password.

tldr.problem: Static passwords and incompatible proprietary token systems made interoperable two-factor authentication difficult. HOTP defines a shared algorithm for producing a short code from a secret and counter.
tldr.mechanism: The client and server use HMAC-SHA-1 on a shared key and an eight-byte counter, then truncate the result to a numeric code. The server uses throttling and a look-ahead window to manage guessing and counter drift.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4226 gives the algorithm and deployment guidance as an Informational RFC. It warns that HOTP does not encrypt traffic or protect its privacy.

today: RFC 4226 is an Informational RFC. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and its text does not specify an Internet standard.

sections.title: Why Define HOTP
sections.content:
RFC 4226 describes one-time passwords based on a shared secret and a changing event counter. Its authors identify weak static passwords and proprietary hardware/software pairings as barriers to broader two-factor authentication.

The document aims to define an algorithm that hardware and software developers can implement in a compatible way. It is intended for a range of network applications, including remote VPN access, Wi-Fi login, and transaction-oriented web applications.
sections.plainLanguage: HOTP gives different devices a common way to produce a one-time password. The RFC aims to make tokens and verification services interoperable.

sections.title: Requirements for the Code
sections.content:
The algorithm must be based on a sequence or counter and work on tokens without numeric input. It should be economical for limited hardware, and the displayed value must be readable and easy to enter.

An HOTP value must have at least six digits. The shared secret must be at least 128 bits; 160 bits is recommended. The system must also provide a user-friendly way to resynchronize the counter.
sections.plainLanguage: The code must be practical for a small token and easy for a person to enter. The RFC also requires a strong shared secret and a way to recover when the counters no longer match.

sections.title: Computing an HOTP Value
sections.content:
The algorithm computes HOTP(K,C) = Truncate(HMAC-SHA-1(K,C)). Here K is the secret shared by the client and server, and C is an eight-byte counter that must be synchronized between them. HMAC-SHA-1 produces a 20-byte result.

Dynamic truncation takes a four-byte part of that result. The low four bits of the final byte select its starting offset; the top bit of the selected four bytes is masked to produce a 31-bit value. The result is reduced modulo 10^Digit to produce the code. Implementations must support at least six digits and may support seven or eight.
sections.plainLanguage: HOTP first mixes the secret and counter into a 20-byte result. It selects part of that result using an offset, then reduces it to the chosen number of digits.

sections.title: Checking Codes and Keeping Counters in Step
sections.content:
The token advances its counter whenever it creates a code. The server advances its counter only after successful validation, so the values can become out of step. The server can check a configured look-ahead window of future counter values to find the submitted code.

Because an attacker can guess a short code, the RFC recommends a server-side attempt limit or increasing delay. Any delay or lockout must apply across login sessions so parallel attempts cannot bypass it. If the maximum number of attempts is reached, the server should lock the account and notify the user.

The RFC also recommends sending authentication over a secure channel. HOTP itself is not a substitute for encryption and does not provide privacy for transmitted data.
sections.plainLanguage: The server can check a limited number of future counter values if the token has moved ahead. It must also limit failed attempts across sessions, and the login exchange needs a secure channel.

sections.title: Security Analysis and Secret Handling
sections.content:
The RFC's analysis treats the truncated outputs for different counters as effectively independent, nearly uniform 31-bit values. It concludes that brute-force guessing is the best attack under its assumptions, with success probability approximated by sv/10^Digit, where s is the look-ahead window and v is the number of verification attempts.

The secret must be protected whether it is derived from a master secret or generated randomly. For deterministic generation, the master key must be kept in a tamper-resistant device. For random generation, the RFC recommends a good random source and secure storage, including encryption at rest. Optional composite secrets can combine a random seed with an additional factor held at the token.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC's security analysis identifies guessing as the main attack and says a larger look-ahead window increases that risk. Protecting the shared secret and limiting attempts are central to safe use.

items.title: 1. HMAC-SHA-1
items.text: Combine the shared key K and counter C into a 20-byte result.

items.title: 2. Dynamic truncation
items.text: Use an offset from the low four bits of the final byte to select a 31-bit value.

items.title: 3. Reduce to digits
items.text: Take the value modulo 10^Digit to obtain the HOTP code.
